content: House dust mites, often abbreviated as HDM by allergists, are microscopic organisms that inhabit human dwellings worldwide. They primarily feed on organic debris, such as flakes of shed human skin, and thrive in the stable indoor environments of homes. In natural settings, they are typically eliminated by micro-predators or exposure to direct sunlight. However, within human habitats, they are a leading cause of asthma and allergic symptoms globally. The enzymes they produce are particularly noticeable in the contents of vacuum cleaner bags. The two most common species of house dust mites are the European house dust mite (Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus) and the American house dust mite (Dermatophagoides farinae). Despite their names, these species are not strictly confined to Europe or North America. Size and Physical Characteristics House dust mites are visible under a magnifying glass when placed on a well-lit black background. They measure approximately 250–320 µm in width and 0.2–0.3 mm in length. Both male and female adult mites are globular in shape, creamy white in color, and possess a striated cuticle. As members of the class Arachnida, they have eight legs in their larval and post-larval stages. Dust mites can become airborne through minor air currents generated by everyday household activities. Life Cycle The average lifespan of a male dust mite is 20–30 days. Mated female dust mites live for approximately 10 weeks, during which they lay 60–100 eggs in the final five weeks of their lives. Over a 10-week lifespan, a single dust mite produces around 2,000 fecal particles and an even greater number of partially digested, enzyme-laden dust particles. Washing fabrics can remove most of this waste material. Temperatures exceeding 60°C (140°F) for one hour or freezing conditions are usually fatal to dust mites. Additionally, a relative humidity below 50% can also lead to their death. Despite their short lifespan, dust mites reproduce rapidly enough to significantly impact human health. Habitat and Feeding Dust mites can survive in nearly all climates, except at high altitudes where reproduction is inhibited. Controlling indoor humidity is crucial for managing dust mites and other water-dependent indoor pathogens. Dust mites thrive in environments where warm, moist air condenses on cooler surfaces, providing the necessary humidity for their survival. When humidity levels drop below optimal conditions, dust mites slow down, become dormant, and may eventually die. These mites are commonly found in beds, kitchens, and other areas of the home where sunlight does not reach. They inhabit mattresses, carpets, furniture, and bedding, where they can burrow deeper into fabrics to avoid sunlight, vacuum cleaners, and other hazards. In dry climates, they still survive and reproduce in bedding, particularly pillows, due to the humidity generated by human breathing and perspiration during sleep. Dust mites consume minute particles of organic matter. Some species prefer skin cells, a major component of household dust, while others favor flour dust. Their alimentary system is rudimentary, lacking a stomach, and most digestion occurs outside their bodies. To facilitate this, they secrete enzymes and deposit the fungus Aspergillus repens on dust particles, which pre-digests the organic matter. Dust mites consume the same particle multiple times, partially digesting it with each feeding. Between feedings, they leave particles to decompose further. Fully digested particles, which mites will not consume again, are classified as fecal matter. Dust mites in bedding derive moisture from human breathing, perspiration, and saliva. Asthma and Allergies House dust mites are among the most common allergens that trigger asthma. Symptoms of dust mite-related allergies include itching, sneezing, inflamed or infected eczema, watery eyes, runny nose, and, in cases of asthma, lung congestion and hay fever.
